the-broken-team-diagnosis.core: When a team underperforms, diagnose before prescribing. Look at clarity of goals, psychological safety, ownership boundaries, process friction, skills and dependencies. Interview people, check metrics (delivery, incidents, attrition), and separate symptoms like missed deadlines from root causes like unclear priorities.

first_principles.problem: Leadership says 'the team is slow' and wants a reorg tomorrow.
derivation: **Map** causes: goals, safety, ownership, process, skills.

analogy.title: A doctor diagnosing before prescribing
analogy.story: Fatigue could be anaemia, stress or thyroid issues, and the treatment differs completely.
analogy.breaks: Patients are one body; teams have multiple interacting causes.

example.title: 'The team is slow'
flow: Fix: quarterly priorities with the PM

check.q: Why not reorganise immediately when a team is slow?
check.a: Slowness has many causes; a reorg may not address the real one and adds disruption.

the-brilliant-jerk-dilemma.core: A highly productive engineer who belittles others often costs more than they produce: colleagues disengage, hide mistakes, avoid their code and leave. Address the behaviour directly and specifically, set clear expectations, and be willing to act. Tolerating it signals that results excuse disrespect.

first_principles.problem: The top contributor's harsh reviews have driven two engineers to transfer out.

analogy.title: A star striker who won't pass
analogy.story: They score some goals, but the team loses more matches.
analogy.breaks: Sports stats show the cost clearly; team damage in engineering is quieter and slower.

example.title: Addressing harsh reviews
flow: Agreed norms: critique code, not people

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Specific and timely beats vague and late.

check.q: Why is tolerating a brilliant jerk costly?
check.a: It reduces psychological safety and drives attrition, lowering the team's total output.

leading-through-crisis-the-war-room.core: In a crisis (major outage, security breach), effective leaders establish clear roles (incident commander, communications, technical leads), a single source of truth, regular updates and calm prioritisation: stabilise first, then fix, then learn. Chaos comes from unclear ownership, not from the problem itself.

first_principles.problem: Thirty people join a call during an outage, all talking, and nobody is deciding.

analogy.title: An air-traffic controller in a storm
analogy.story: One calm voice sequences everything; pilots follow clear instructions.
analogy.breaks: Controllers follow strict protocols; incidents often need improvisation within the structure.

example.title: Payment outage
flow: IC declared, roles assigned in 5 min

check.q: What's the incident commander's main job?
check.a: Coordinate and decide: assign roles, set priorities and keep the response organised, not debug personally.

turning-around-a-demotivated-team.core: Demotivation usually comes from loss of autonomy, mastery or purpose (Daniel Pink): constant firefighting, no say in decisions, unclear impact. Turn it around by listening, removing the biggest frustrations, delivering quick wins, reconnecting work to impact, and giving genuine ownership.

first_principles.problem: A team after layoffs and a failed project shows low energy, missed commitments and quiet attrition.
truths: Motivation needs autonomy, mastery and purpose.

analogy.title: Reviving a neglected garden
analogy.story: Clear the weeds, water consistently, and let the first flowers show what's possible.
analogy.breaks: Gardens don't resent past neglect; people need trust rebuilt explicitly.

example.title: Post-layoff team
flow: Week 3–6: kill flaky pipeline, cut meetings 30%
Week 7–12: team owns roadmap item, demo to users

check.q: What three drivers of motivation does Daniel Pink describe?

the-blameless-post-mortem.core: A blameless postmortem asks how the system allowed the failure, not who caused it. Engineers acted reasonably given what they knew, so fixes target process, tooling and safeguards. Blame makes people hide information; blamelessness surfaces the truth needed to prevent recurrence.

first_principles.problem: After an outage, an engineer is reprimanded, and the next incident is hidden for hours.
truths: Humans make errors in complex systems.

analogy.title: Aviation safety investigations
analogy.story: They aim to prevent the next crash, not punish the pilot, so crews report near-misses freely.
analogy.breaks: Blameless doesn't mean accountability-free: negligence and repeated disregard still matter.

example.title: Accidental production table drop
flow: Blameless: why could a dev credential drop prod tables?
Factors: shared creds, no confirmation, no backups test
Actions: role separation, guarded CLI, restore drills

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No one can repeat the mistake.

check.q: Why does blame make systems less reliable?
check.a: People hide mistakes and information, so problems surface late and root causes stay unfixed.
